# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Supervised machine learning comprises a collection of algorithms that map feature matrices to responses: estimating a function $\hat{f}: \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}$ (regression) or $\hat{f}: \mathbb{R}^p \to \{1,\ldots,K\}$ (classification) that generalises well to new data [@HastieEtAl2009]. Applied workflows inevitably involve more than a single fit-and-predict call. Practitioners need resampling-based performance estimation, hyperparameter search, multi-learner benchmarks, post-hoc interpretation, and increasingly links between predictive models and causal questions.

In R, these tasks are scattered across multiple frameworks. `caret` [@Kuhn2008] standardised model fitting and resampling under one interface but has largely been superseded. `mlr3` [@Lang2019] provides a powerful object-oriented system based on R6 with a rich ecosystem of extensions. `tidymodels` [@tidymodels2019] integrates with the tidyverse and offers deep preprocessing support. `iml` [@Molnar2018] unifies model-agnostic interpretation. Each of these is excellent within its design space, but combining them across a single analysis requires navigating incompatible object systems and learning several different programming paradigms.

The **funcml** package [@funcml_pkg] was built for a different point in the design space: a compact, formula-first framework that keeps machine learning close to native R modeling conventions while supporting the full applied workflow through a small number of stable verbs.

::: callout-note
## Design philosophy

**funcml** is intentionally opinionated. Preprocessing---imputation, encoding, scaling---is expected to happen *before* any `funcml` call. The package provides modeling, not pipeline orchestration. This keeps the API surface small and function arguments transparent: every input to `fit()` or `evaluate()` is visible in the call.
:::

The interface revolves around six verbs (Table [-@tbl-verbs]), each returning a stable S3 object with consistent `print()`, `summary()`, and `plot()` methods.

| Verb                 | Purpose                       | Returns           |
|----------------------|-------------------------------|-------------------|
| `fit()`              | Train a model                 | `funcml_fit`      |
| `evaluate()`         | Resampling-based performance  | `funcml_eval`     |
| `tune()`             | Hyperparameter search         | `funcml_tune`     |
| `compare_learners()` | Multi-learner benchmarking    | `funcml_compare`  |
| `interpret()`        | Model-agnostic interpretation | method-specific   |
| `estimate()`         | Plug-in g-computation         | `funcml_estimand` |

: Core **funcml** verbs and their return classes. {#tbl-verbs}

This tutorial walks through each verb in order. @sec-install covers installation and introduces the running datasets. @sec-workflow gives a visual overview of the complete pipeline. @sec-resampling introduces resampling generators, which underpin evaluation, tuning, and comparison. @sec-learners presents all 23 learners with statistical foundations and R code. @sec-metrics covers the metric library. @sec-eval through @sec-compare demonstrate evaluation, tuning, and benchmarking. @sec-interpret covers all fourteen interpretation methods. @sec-estimate presents g-computation for causal effect estimation. @sec-e2e ties everything together in a single end-to-end example.

**Notation.** Throughout, $n$ denotes sample size; $p$ the number of features; $\mathbf{x}_i = (x_{i1}, \ldots, x_{ip})^\top \in
\mathbb{R}^p$ the feature vector of observation $i$; and $y_i$ the scalar response. $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$ denotes the full feature matrix and $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ the response vector. $\hat{f}$ always refers to the estimated prediction function.

# Installation and Datasets {#sec-install}

## Installation

**funcml** is available from GitHub and can be installed with:

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
remotes::install_github("ielbadisy/funcml")
```

```{r load}
library(funcml)
```

## Datasets

**funcml** ships with fifteen curated datasets covering regression, binary classification, and multiclass classification. The full list can be inspected at any time:

```{r dataset-list, eval=FALSE}
data(package = "funcml")
```

Throughout this tutorial we use three representative datasets that together cover the three main supervised learning tasks.

**Birthweight (regression).** The `birthweight` dataset [@HosmerLemeshow1989] contains 189 mother–infant pairs. The outcome is birth weight in grams (`birth_weight_g`); predictors include maternal age, pre-pregnancy weight, race, smoking status, and obstetric history.

```{r data-reg}
data_reg   <- birthweight
formula_reg <- birth_weight_g ~ age + lwt + race + smoke + ptl + ht + ui + ftv
dim(data_reg)
```

**Pima Diabetes (binary classification).** The `pimadiabetes` dataset [@Smith1988] contains 532 patients from the Pima Indian Diabetes Database. The outcome is a diabetes diagnosis indicator (`diabetes`; `"Yes"` / `"No"`). We use the pre-specified training partition and discard the split indicator.[^1]

[^1]: The original Pima Indians dataset was collected by the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases. Only female patients aged at least 21 years were included.

```{r data-cls}
data_cls   <- pimadiabetes[pimadiabetes$split == "train", ]
data_cls   <- data_cls[, setdiff(names(data_cls), "split")]
formula_cls <- diabetes ~ npreg + glu + bp + skin + bmi + ped + age
dim(data_cls)
table(data_cls$diabetes)
```

**Thyroid Function (multiclass).** The `newthyroid` dataset contains 215 patients classified as normal (1), hyperthyroid (2), or hypothyroid (3) based on five thyroid laboratory measurements.

```{r data-mc}
data_mc   <- newthyroid
data_mc$class <- factor(data_mc$class)
formula_mc <- class ~ t3_resin_uptake + total_serum_thyroxin +
  total_serum_triiodothyronine + basal_tsh + max_abs_tsh_diff
dim(data_mc)
table(data_mc$class)
```

With the package loaded and data prepared, we next describe how these pieces fit together into a coherent analysis pipeline.

# The funcml Workflow {#sec-workflow}

The **funcml** pipeline flows from raw data through a fitted model to performance assessment, interpretation, and causal estimation. Each stage corresponds to one of the six top-level verbs introduced in @sec-intro.

```{r workflow-diagram, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="The complete funcml analysis pipeline. Arrows indicate data flow; every stage returns a structured S3 object that feeds the next.", fig.height=2.2, fig.width=8}
stages <- data.frame(
  x     = c(0.8, 2.5, 4.2, 5.9, 7.6, 9.3),
  label = c("Data", "fit()", "evaluate()\ntune()", "compare_\nlearners()", "interpret()", "estimate()"),
  type  = c("data", "core", "core", "core", "interp", "causal")
)
cols <- c(data = "#6baed6", core = "#2171b5", interp = "#238b45", causal = "#8c510a")

ggplot(stages, aes(x, 0)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = type), width = 1.35, height = 0.55, color = "white", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), size = 2.85, color = "white", fontface = "bold", lineheight = 0.88) +
  annotate("segment",
           x    = c(1.48, 3.18, 4.88, 6.58, 8.28),
           xend = c(1.82, 3.52, 5.22, 6.92, 8.62),
           y = 0, yend = 0,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm"), type = "closed"),
           color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cols) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.5, 0.5)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 10.1)) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        plot.margin = margin(4, 4, 4, 4))
```

The package follows a **preprocessing-outside** design: data passed to any `funcml` verb is exactly the data that will be modelled. There are no hidden transformations, no formula preprocessing pipelines, and no implicit encoding steps. This transparency is deliberate , it keeps the function arguments self-documenting and avoids hidden state that can cause silent errors between training and prediction.[^2]

[^2]: Users who need graph-based preprocessing or formula-level feature engineering can combine `funcml` with base R helpers (e.g., `model.matrix()`, `scale()`) before passing data to `fit()`. Larger preprocessing ecosystems such as `mlr3pipelines` [@Binder2021] or `recipes` [@tidymodels2019] remain compatible with this approach.

The learner registry and all available metrics and interpretation methods can be queried at runtime, making the package self-documenting:

```{r registry}
list_learners() |> head(8)
```

```{r metrics-list}
list_metrics() |> head(8)
```

```{r interp-list}
list_interpretability_methods()
```

The first concrete design choice in any analysis is how to partition the data for honest performance estimation. That is where the tutorial begins.

# Resampling Strategies {#sec-resampling}

## Theory

Performance on training data is an optimistic estimate of generalisation performance because the model has already seen the training observations. The standard remedy is to hold out data during training, evaluate on the held-out portion, and repeat in a systematic way. Formally, given a dataset $\mathcal{D} = \{(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$, the goal is to estimate the expected prediction error:

$$
\text{Err} = \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x}, y),\, \mathcal{D}}
\bigl[L\!\bigl(y,\, \hat{f}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{x})\bigr)\bigr]
$$

where $L$ is a loss function and $\hat{f}_{\mathcal{D}}$ is the model trained on $\mathcal{D}$ [@HastieEtAl2009].

$K$-fold cross-validation [@Stone1974] partitions $\mathcal{D}$ into $K$ folds of roughly equal size. The model is trained on $K-1$ folds and evaluated on the held-out fold, rotating until every observation has served as a validation observation exactly once:

$$
\widehat{\text{CV}}(K)
= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n
  L\!\bigl(y_i,\, \hat{f}^{-\kappa(i)}(\mathbf{x}_i)\bigr)
$$

where $\kappa(i)$ maps observation $i$ to its fold and $\hat{f}^{-\kappa(i)}$ is the model trained on all folds except $\kappa(i)$. Setting $K = n$ gives leave-one-out CV (LOO-CV).[^3] Common choices are $K = 5$ and $K = 10$.

[^3]: LOO-CV is nearly unbiased for the true error but has high variance and is computationally expensive for large $n$. For most practical purposes, $K = 5$ or $K = 10$ offers a good bias-variance tradeoff [@HastieEtAl2009].

**Holdout validation** reserves a fixed fraction $\pi \in (0, 1)$ of observations for testing. While computationally cheap, it is high-variance: performance depends heavily on the particular random split, especially when $n$ is small.

**Grouped cross-validation** ensures that observations sharing a group identifier , patients, hospitals, geographic clusters , are never split across folds. Without this constraint, leakage between correlated observations produces optimistic estimates.

**Time-series cross-validation** respects the temporal order of observations by expanding or rolling the training window. Fold $k$ trains on $\{1, \ldots, t_k\}$ and evaluates on $\{t_k+1, \ldots, t_k+h\}$ for an assessment horizon $h$, preventing future data from informing past predictions.

```{r cv-diagram, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Schematic of 5-fold cross-validation. Each row is one fold iteration: grey tiles are training observations, blue tiles are held-out validation observations.", fig.height=2.4, fig.width=6.5}
n_obs  <- 20
n_fold <- 5
fold_id <- rep(1:n_fold, length.out = n_obs)
df <- expand.grid(fold = 1:n_fold, obs = 1:n_obs)
df$role <- ifelse(df$fold == df$obs %% n_fold + 1, "Validation", "Training")
ggplot(df, aes(x = obs, y = fold, fill = role)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Training = "#bdc9e1", Validation = "#2171b5")) +
  scale_y_reverse(breaks = 1:n_fold, labels = paste("Fold", 1:n_fold)) +
  labs(x = "Observation index", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid = element_blank())
```

## funcml Resampling Constructors

All four strategies are created with dedicated constructors that return objects accepted by `evaluate()`, `tune()`, and `compare_learners()` without modification:

```{r resampling-demo}
cv5   <- cv(v = 5, seed = 42)              # 5-fold CV
cv5r  <- cv(v = 5, repeats = 3, seed = 42) # repeated CV
ho    <- holdout(prop = 0.8, seed = 42)    # 80/20 holdout
# group_cv(v = 5, group = "patient_id")   # grouped CV
# time_cv(initial = 50, assess = 10)      # time-series CV
```

::: callout-tip
## Choosing a resampling strategy

Use **5-fold CV** as the default. Increase to 10 folds when $n < 200$. Use **repeated CV** when you need low-variance estimates of confidence intervals. Use **grouped CV** whenever observations within a group are correlated (e.g., repeat measurements, clustered designs). Use **holdout** only when $n$ is large enough that a single split is stable (roughly $n > 2000$).
:::

With a resampling strategy in hand, we can now explore the learners available in the registry.

# The Learner Registry {#sec-learners}

## Overview

The **funcml** registry contains 23 learners spanning ten algorithmic families (Table [-@tbl-registry]). All are accessed through a string identifier passed to `model =`. The registry is queryable and extensible: `list_learners()` returns a data frame of all learners with columns for task compatibility, probability output, multiclass support, native feature importance, and tunable hyperparameters.

| Learner ID     | Algorithm                          | Task     | Engine       |

| `glmnet`       | Elastic Net                        | Reg, Cls | glmnet       |
